record.tranche_reason: Applies transcoder/SAE feature analysis in a vision-language model and reports recovered task-related features, extending indirect feature evidence to a VLM setting.
record.gate_note: The sequential Stroop behavior results do not test the listed superposition versions. The feature-analysis results bear on V4; the paper does not test feature-capacity competition, canonicality or stability of SAE units, or one-dimensional feature geometry. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study applies off-the-shelf Qwen3 4B transcoders to InternVL 3.5 4B as a tool to locate Stroop-related supernodes. It does not ask whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or recoverable by a dictionary. It reports no reconstruction quality, no neuron-level polysemanticity, and no comparison with a non-SAE baseline. Its questions are conflict adaptation and its mechanism, not superposition, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The main conclusion is behavioral: 12 of 13 VLMs show conflict adaptation (II > CI in log probability of the correct second color), and the exception, Qwen2.5 VL 72B, is attributed to a ceiling effect. The supernode findings are offered as the representational basis. Ablating the conflict supernode raises Stroop errors 3.38-fold on CI trials and 8.33-fold on II trials, with minimal effect on congruent trials.
record.recipe_differences: Uses transcoders (described as an SAE variant) and coactivation-based grouping in a pretrained VLM, rather than testing toy networks with the original superposition method.

fits_no_version.finding: Conflict-modulated transcoder features in layers 24-25 are dense, activating across diverse contexts, and lack clear interpretations. Color and text features, by contrast, are sparse and interpretable. Ablating the conflict supernode raises errors from 17.5% to 59.2% on CI trials and from 2.5% to 20.8% on II trials.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transcoder features that are causally important can be dense and uninterpretable, rather than sparse monosemantic units.

record.problems: Feature analysis is limited to one model and the reported red color/text features. The authors note that they apply base-language-model transcoders to a VLM with modified weights, which introduces potential concerns. No uncertainty estimates are stated for these feature results.
record.rows_left_out: Behavioral conflict-adaptation results and the conflict-supernode ablation were left out because they do not measure any listed superposition version. No other results bearing on V4 were reported.

untested.parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity transition, geometry: not studied.
Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity: not studied.
Transcoders are used as a tool. Neither feature spreading across neurons nor dictionary recovery quality is measured.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of dictionary features: not studied. Transfer of base-LM transcoders to modified VLM weights is only argued for, via ablation.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The SAE/transcoder analysis relies on dictionary features being meaningful and does not evaluate that premise. The authors concede that applying base-LM transcoders to a VLM with modified weights raises concerns, and support the transfer only through ablation. Preprint, single author.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature importance and capacity competition cause dedicated dimensions or sharing.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Does not establish that features are generally spread across neurons in LLMs; examines task-relevant features in one pretrained VLM using transcoders.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of dictionary features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions.

rows.subject: InternVL 3.5 4B (pretrained)
rows.operation_detail: Used transcoders and coactivation-based grouping to identify red-color supernodes.
rows.measure: Recovered supernodes and their layer spans
rows.value: Two supernodes: one in layers 8-11 and one in layers 19-33; the text and color supernodes partially overlap in early and late layers.
rows.note: The authors describe the color and text features as sparse and interpretable; top activating texts largely mention the corresponding colors.
rows.check: Layer spans of a red-color supernode found with pretrained transcoders are a task-mechanism finding. They do not measure whether features are spread across neurons or how well the dictionary recovers sparse features.

rows.subject: InternVL 3.5 4B (pretrained)
rows.operation_detail: Used transcoders and coactivation-based grouping to identify RED-text supernodes.
rows.measure: Recovered supernodes and their layer spans
rows.value: Two supernodes: one in layers 3-15 and one in layers 19-33; the text and color supernodes partially overlap in early and late layers.
rows.note: The authors report that the early text supernode contains more features than the early color supernode, while the late color supernode contains more than the late text supernode.
rows.check: Same issue as r1: layer spans and overlap of the RED-text supernode describe a task mechanism, not evidence about superposition or SAE recovery.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Assumes dictionary decomposition is useful and applies it to conflict adaptation, without evaluating superposition, dictionary completeness, stability, or canonicality.

tranche.reason: Uses pretrained transcoders and feature coactivation as tools to identify Stroop mechanisms; the reported layer spans and ablations do not test a superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: The authors acknowledge transferring Qwen3 4B transcoders to modified VLM weights; causal ablations support functional relevance. The study text is arXiv v2, dated 18 November 2025.
